Welcome. Today is about how a drone flies and how we're building one. Our first prototype spun its props and skated across the floor, but it never lifted off. We worked out why, and the second prototype, with a different motor driver, is being built now. We'll start with the physics, then our two prototypes, the firmware, and finally how a full 6S racing drone differs.

Introduction to
drone technology

Here is the route for today, five stops climbing from theory to flight. First the physics of how four motors steer a quad. Then our micro build on an ESP32, including the driver that failed and the MOSFET fix. Then the firmware: the 500 hertz loop, the PID controller, the motor mixer and the radio links. Then we scale up to a five-inch FPV racer with brushless motors, DShot and 6S power. And finally how to fly safely: bench rules, flight modes and PID tuning.

01

Drone basics

A drone is any aircraft that flies without a pilot on board. Four families cover almost everything you will see. Multirotors, like quadcopters and hexacopters, can hover and are mechanically simple, but they burn energy just to stay up, so flights are short. Fixed-wing drones fly like aeroplanes: the wing makes the lift, so they fly far and long, but they cannot hover and need space to launch and land. Hybrid VTOL drones take off vertically like a multirotor and then cruise on a wing, which gives you both, at the cost of complexity. Single-rotor helicopters lift heavy loads efficiently but are mechanically the most complex. Today we focus on multirotors, because they are the easiest to build and the best way to learn the control problem.

Drone basics

What counts as a drone

Any aircraft that flies with no pilot on board. Four families cover almost everything in the sky.

Multirotor

Hovers, simple mechanics, easy to control. Short flights, since the motors carry all the weight. Today's focus.

Fixed-wing

The wing makes the lift, so it flies far and long. Cannot hover; needs room to launch and land.

Hybrid VTOL

Takes off like a multirotor, cruises like a plane. Best of both, with more complexity.

Single-rotor

Helicopter layout. Lifts heavy loads efficiently; the most complex mechanics.

Drones are working tools now, which is why they matter to mechanical engineers. Farmers use them to spray crops and to spot stressed plants with special cameras. Surveyors fly them to build maps and 3D models of land and buildings in hours instead of weeks. Engineers use them to inspect power lines, bridges and wind turbines without climbing. They deliver medicines to places roads do not reach, help search teams after disasters, and are used heavily in defence. And in film and sport, FPV drones capture shots no crane can. Every one of these is a mechanical design problem first: weight, stiffness, vibration, endurance and payload.

Every one of these is a mechanical design problem first: weight, stiffness, vibration, endurance, payload.

This is the mechanical side. The frame has to be light but stiff, because any flex or vibration goes straight into the gyro and confuses the controller. That is why racers use carbon fibre and why we mount the sensor at the centre. Propeller size sets the frame size: a five-inch prop needs a frame of roughly 220 millimetres across so the props do not touch. Thrust-to-weight is the number that decides how it flies: around two to one to hover with control left over, and racers go far higher. And flight time is a weight budget: every extra gram has to be held up by the motors for the whole flight, so battery size, frame weight and payload all trade against each other.

Drone basics

The mechanical side

Frame: light, but stiff

Flex and vibration go straight into the gyro. Carbon fibre for racers, printed or aluminium frames for builds like ours.

Props set the size

A 5-inch prop needs a frame about 220 mm across so the props never touch.

Thrust-to-weight

About 2 : 1 to hover with control to spare. Racing quads go far beyond that.

Flight time is a weight budget

Every gram is carried by the motors for the whole flight. Battery, frame and payload trade against each other.

A quadcopter steers only by changing how fast each motor spins. The orange props spin clockwise and the teal ones counter-clockwise: M1 front left spins clockwise, M2 front right counter-clockwise, M3 rear right clockwise, M4 rear left counter-clockwise. Neighbours spin opposite ways so their torques cancel and the frame doesn't spin on its own. To roll right, the left pair speeds up. To pitch nose down and fly forward, the rear pair speeds up. To yaw right, the counter-clockwise pair, M2 and M4, speeds up and its reaction torque turns the frame. Throttle is all four together. Hovering needs thrust equal to weight; aim for about 2:1 so there's room left for control.

Roll right. M1 and M4, the two motors on the left, spin faster. The left side lifts, the drone leans right, and part of its thrust now pushes it sideways, so it slides right.

Now the opposite. M2 and M3 on the right side speed up, the right side lifts, and the drone leans and slides left.

Pitch forward. The rear pair, M3 and M4, speeds up. The tail rises, the nose dips, and the tilted thrust pulls the drone forward.

Pitch back is the mirror image. The front pair, M1 and M2, speeds up, the nose comes up, and the drone moves backward.

Flight physics

How four motors steer a quad

Orange props spin clockwise, teal props counter-clockwise. Click to step through roll, pitch, yaw and climb.

Before anything flies, the props have to match the motors. Clockwise motors, M1 front left and M3 rear right, take clockwise props. Counter-clockwise motors, M2 and M4, take counter-clockwise props. You can tell them apart by the blade: the raised, thicker edge goes first in the direction of rotation, like a wing leading into the air. Props come in matched pairs, so check the arrow or letter printed on them too. Quick test: spin each prop by hand the way its motor turns and feel for air going down. Put one on backwards and that corner pushes air up, and the drone flips the moment it tries to take off.

These are our two drones. Both use an ESP32, an MPU-6050, four 8520 coreless motors and a single LiPo cell, and both run firmware we customised from Espressif's official ESP-Drone firmware. The only difference is the motor driver. Prototype 1 used two DRV8833 H-bridge boards. It spun its props but never lifted off. Prototype 2 replaces them with four AO3400 MOSFETs, one per motor, and we're still building it.

Two prototypes

Our two drones

Both use an ESP32 running firmware customised from Espressif's official ESP-Drone firmware, an MPU-6050, four 8520 coreless motors and a 1S LiPo. Only the motor driver is different.

Prototype 1 DRV8833

Two DRV8833 H-bridge boards drive the motors. Built and tested: the props spun, but it skated across the floor and never lifted off.

Prototype 2 AO3400

One AO3400 MOSFET per motor, four in total. Designed, and being built now.

02

The micro build

Here's what goes on the quad. The ESP32 DevKit is the brain: dual core at 240 MHz, and one core runs the 500 Hz flight loop. The MPU-6050 gives us a three-axis gyro and accelerometer over I2C at 400 kHz, and it sits at the centre of gravity so rotation doesn't show up as false acceleration. The 8520 coreless motors are 8.5 by 20 mm, about 5 g each, on 55 mm props. In prototype 2 each motor gets its own AO3400 MOSFET, switched at 16 kHz. Power is one LiPo cell with a TP4056 USB charger, a 5 V boost so the ESP32 doesn't brown out, and a 100k/100k divider so we can read the battery voltage on GPIO 34.

One low-side MOSFET per motor, 16 kHz PWM.

8.5 × 20 mm, about 5 g each, 55 mm props.

Prototype 1 had the same ESP32, IMU, motors and battery, with two DRV8833 H-bridge boards driving the motors. At full throttle the props spun, but the quad only skated across the floor. It never lifted off. At the motor terminals we read under 2.7 V from a 3.7 V battery, so about a volt was going missing somewhere.

The roadblock

Prototype 1 never
left the floor

< 2.7 V

reached the motors (measured), from a battery rated 3.7 V.

The motors were driven by two DRV8833 H-bridge boards. At full throttle the props spun, but the quad only skated across the floor. It never lifted off.

Follow the current. Inside each DRV8833 channel it passes through a high-side and a low-side transistor, about 360 milliohms in total according to TI's datasheet. At full throttle an 8520 motor wants 3.5 to 4 A. Ohm's law: 3.5 A times 0.36 ohm is about 1.3 V dropped inside the chip, so it never reaches the motor. The chip is also rated for only 1.5 A RMS per channel. With less voltage the motors can't spin fast enough to lift the quad. H-bridge chips like this are made for toy-car motors that run in both directions at under an amp. A drone motor turns one way and needs a lot more current.

Diagnosis

Where the missing volt went

3.5 A × 0.36 Ω ≈ 1.3 V lost inside the chip, never reaches the motor

Driver limit

1.5 A RMS, 2 A peak per channel (TI datasheet)

Motor demand

8520s pull 3.5–4.2 A at full throttle

Not enough lift

Less voltage at the motor, so the props can't lift the quad

Prototype 2 swaps the H-bridge for one N-channel MOSFET per motor. Read the diagram left to right: current leaves the battery, goes through the motor, then through the MOSFET, and into ground. The MOSFET is just a switch. The ESP32 turns it on and off 16,000 times a second, and the share of time it's on sets the motor speed. Three parts make it work. The AO3400 is logic-level, so the ESP32's 3.3 V turns it fully on, with tens of milliohms of resistance and a 5.7 A rating. A 10 k resistor from gate to ground keeps it off while the ESP32 boots, so the motors can't twitch at power-up. And the SS24 diode across the motor gives the motor's current somewhere to go when the switch opens, so there's no voltage spike. Motors 1 to 4 use GPIO 32, 25, 33 and 26.

The fix

One MOSFET per motor

1 AO3400 N-channel MOSFET

Logic-level: a 3.3 V gate turns it fully on. Tens of milliohms, 5.7 A continuous.

2 10 kΩ gate pull-down

Holds the motor off while the ESP32 boots and its pins float.

3 SS24 Schottky diode

Gives the motor current a path when the switch opens, so there is no voltage spike.

Pins from Drone/src/config.h: M1 GPIO 32, M2 GPIO 25, M3 GPIO 33, M4 GPIO 26. 16 kHz, 12-bit LEDC PWM.

Here's what should change. The DRV8833 path is about 360 milliohms; the MOSFET is tens of milliohms, roughly ten times less. The DRV8833 is rated 1.5 A RMS; the AO3400 handles 5.7 A continuous. At 3.5 A through about 50 milliohms we'd lose around 0.2 V, so we expect roughly 3.5 V at the motor. That's a calculation, not a measurement, because prototype 2 isn't built yet. Same motors, same battery, same code: only the driver changes. Once it's built, the first thing we'll do is put a multimeter on the motor terminals.

03

The firmware

Now the firmware. The ESP32 has two cores. Core zero runs the Wi-Fi and ESP-NOW radio stack, which receives stick packets and turns them into setpoints. Core one runs our flight task every two milliseconds, five hundred times a second, at high priority: read the IMU, fuse the readings into an attitude estimate, run the PID controller, mix the corrections into four motor outputs, and write the PWM. Also on core one, at low priority, the normal Arduino loop handles serial and web commands, telemetry and the blackbox log, battery and LED, and a watchdog that cuts the motors if the flight task goes silent for fifty milliseconds. The rule that keeps this safe is that only the flight task ever touches I2C and the motors; everything else talks to it through small locked shared buffers.

Firmware

Two cores, one 500 Hz flight loop

Core 0 · Wi-Fi and ESP-NOW stack

The radio receives stick packets from the remote or phone app and hands over setpoints.

Core 1 · flight task, every 2 ms
Read IMU
Fuse attitude
PID

PWM out
Core 1 · loop(), low priority

Serial and web commands · telemetry and blackbox · battery and LED · motor watchdog cuts power if the flight task is silent for 50 ms

Rule: only the flight task touches I²C and the motors. Everything else talks to it through locked shared data.

Inside each two millisecond tick, the controller is a cascade of two loops. The pilot's stick becomes a target angle, at most thirty degrees. The outer angle loop compares that with the estimated angle and multiplies the error by four to get a target rotation rate, capped at two hundred degrees per second. The inner rate loop is a full PID that compares the target rate with what the gyro measures. The mixer then turns roll, pitch and yaw corrections into four motor commands. The angle estimate comes from a complementary filter: we trust the gyro 99.5 percent because it is smooth, and the accelerometer half a percent because it knows which way is down but is noisy. If the accelerometer reads far from one g, during a hard manoeuvre, we ignore it. Two more details: the D term acts on the measurement so a stick jump does not kick the motors, and the I term is frozen below fifteen percent throttle so it does not wind up on the ground.

Control loop

Inside every 2 ms tick

Stick → target angle (max 30°) → angle loop P × 4 → target rate (max 200°/s) → rate PID against the gyro → mixer → motors

Complementary filter, live
angle = 0.995·(angle + gyro·dt) + 0.005·accel

grey = gyro alone drifts · teal = accel alone is noisy · orange = fused

There are three ways to talk to this drone. A handheld remote, another ESP32, sends ESP-NOW packets on Wi-Fi channel one, peer to peer, no router needed. Each packet is thirteen bytes: a magic number, a sequence counter, throttle from zero to a thousand, and roll, pitch and yaw from minus five hundred to plus five hundred, plus a flags byte where bit zero is the arm switch. Second, the drone runs its own Wi-Fi access point at 192.168.43.42, so the ESP-Drone phone app can fly it over UDP port 2390. To arm from the app you bring throttle to zero after connecting and then raise it. Third, a web dashboard shows live telemetry, lets you tune PID gains, and runs bench tests while disarmed. Whatever the link, if no packet arrives for 500 milliseconds while armed, the drone disarms itself.

Radio links

That is our micro quad. Now let us scale up to a five-inch FPV racer. The physics does not change at all. What changes is everything around it: brushless motors instead of brushed ones, an electronic speed controller speaking a digital protocol instead of a simple MOSFET, and a six-cell battery at 22.2 volts instead of a single 3.7 volt cell.

04

Scaling up to
a 5-inch racer

Here is a racer taken apart, layer by layer. On top, a 6S LiPo, typically around 1300 milliamp hours with a high C rating. Below it the ExpressLRS receiver on 2.4 gigahertz, which can send up to a thousand packets a second at short range, trading rate for range. Then the flight controller, an STM32 F7 or H7 running Betaflight with a low-noise gyro such as the ICM-42688, running its gyro and PID loop at eight kilohertz, sixteen times faster than ours. Under that, a four-in-one ESC rated 45 to 60 amps per motor, speaking DShot600. At the bottom, a five-inch carbon frame with 2207 motors, usually 1750 to 1960 KV on six cells.

FPV stack

A racer, layer by layer

6S LiPo

22.2 V nominal, ~1300 mAh, 120 C

ExpressLRS receiver

2.4 GHz, up to 1000 packets/s at short range

Flight controller

STM32 F7/H7, Betaflight, 8 kHz gyro + PID loop

4-in-1 ESC

45–60 A per motor, DShot600 + RPM telemetry

2207 motors

1750–1960 KV on 6S, 5-inch carbon frame

Our brushed motors have carbon brushes that rub on a commutator, so they wear out, but they are cheap and need only simple on-off PWM, which is perfect under sixty grams. Brushless motors have no brushes; the ESC switches three phases electronically, a typical racer motor has twelve coils and fourteen magnets, and only the bearings wear. The name 2207 is just the stator size: 22 millimetres in diameter, 7 millimetres tall. Wider gives more torque, taller gives more top-end speed. KV means RPM per volt with no load, so a 1960 KV motor on a 22.2 volt pack spins at about 43,500 RPM unloaded, and slower under the load of a propeller. That is why six-cell builds use lower KV and four-cell builds use higher KV.

Motors

Brushless, and what KV means

No brushes. The ESC energises the 12 stator coils in three phases, pulling the 14 magnets in the bell around. Only the bearings wear.

2207 = 22 mm stator diameter, 7 mm tall.

1960 KV × 22.2 V
≈ 43,500
RPM with no load

Older ESC protocols encoded throttle as the width of a pulse, between one and two milliseconds. That analog timing drifts and needs calibration. DShot sends throttle as a number. Each frame is sixteen bits: eleven bits of throttle, where 48 to 2047 is throttle and 1 to 47 are special commands, one bit to request telemetry, and a four-bit checksum, so corrupted frames are thrown away. At 600 kilobits per second a frame takes just under 27 microseconds. Two extras matter for flying. Bidirectional DShot lets the ESC send motor RPM back on the same wire, and Betaflight uses that to place notch filters exactly on the motor noise. Active braking lets the ESC slow the prop down instead of letting it coast, so the quad responds and settles faster.

ESC protocol

DShot sends throttle as a number

One DShot600 frame: throttle 1046

11 throttle bits (48–2047)T4-bit checksum
26.7 µs

16 bits at 600 kbit/s

Bidirectional DShot

The ESC replies with motor RPM on the same wire. Betaflight notches out exactly that motor noise.

Active braking

The ESC brakes the prop when throttle drops, so the quad responds and settles faster.

Why did racers move from four cells to six? Power is voltage times current. For the same thousand-watt punch, a 4S pack at 14.8 volts must deliver about 68 amps, while a 6S pack at 22.2 volts needs only about 45. Heat in the wires and in the cells grows with current squared times resistance, so a third less current means far less heat and far less voltage sag. To know what a pack can deliver, multiply capacity by C rating: a 1.3 amp-hour pack rated 120 C gives 156 amps continuous. Pull more and the cells puff up and age quickly. And protect your electronics: a low-ESR capacitor across the ESC pads, for example a thousand microfarads rated 35 volts or more, with 50 volts giving extra margin on 6S, and optionally a TVS diode to clamp the spikes that active braking pushes back into the battery line.

Power

Why racers moved from 4S to 6S

4S · 14.8 V

0 A

for a 1000 W punch-out

same power, less heat, less sag

Current a pack can give

capacity × C: 1.3 Ah × 120 C = 156 A

Protect the electronics

Low-ESR cap on the ESC pads (1000 µF, 35 V+; 50 V gives margin on 6S). A TVS diode clamps braking spikes.

05

Fly safely

Before anything flies, four rules. First, props off on the bench, always; a motor that spins up unexpectedly can cut you in milliseconds. Second, use a smoke stopper, a resettable fuse in the battery lead, the first time you power a new build, so a short trips the fuse instead of burning the board. Third, check for shorts with a multimeter across battery positive and ground before plugging in; you should never see a near-zero reading. Fourth, test the failsafe: with the drone disarmed, switch the radio off and confirm the drone stays disarmed. Our own firmware enforces the same ideas. Motor tests are locked until you type props off, which unlocks them for five minutes. Tests and settings changes only run while disarmed. No radio packet for 500 milliseconds while armed disarms the drone, and if the flight task stops for 50 milliseconds, the main loop cuts the motors.

Bench safety

Four rules before every power-up

  1. Props off on the bench.
    A surprise spin-up cuts in milliseconds.
  2. Smoke stopper on first power-up.
    A resettable fuse trips before a short burns the board.
  3. Check for shorts first.
    Multimeter across VBAT and GND: no near-zero reading.
  4. Test the failsafe.
    Disarmed, radio off: the drone must stay disarmed.

Our firmware enforces it too

Motor tests stay locked until you type props off, which unlocks them for 5 minutes.

Tests and setting changes run only while disarmed.

No radio for 500 ms while armed: it disarms.

Flight task silent for 50 ms: loop() cuts the motors.

There are two main ways a flight controller reads your sticks. In Angle mode the stick sets a tilt angle, at most thirty degrees in our firmware, and when you let go the drone levels itself using the gyro and the accelerometer. That's the mode our ESP32 firmware uses, and it's where every beginner should start. In Acro, or rate mode, the stick sets how fast the drone rotates, for example 670 degrees per second at full stick, and when you let go it holds whatever attitude it's in, even upside down. It uses only the gyro, and it's what makes flips and racing possible. Learn in Angle, then practise Acro in a simulator before trying real flips.

Flight modes

Angle mode, then Acro mode

Angle: self-levelling

The stick sets a tilt angle, at most 30° on our firmware. Let go and it levels itself using gyro and accelerometer. Start here.

Acro: rate mode

The stick sets rotation speed, around 670°/s at full stick. Let go and it holds its attitude, even upside down. Gyro only.

Learn in Angle, then practise Acro in a simulator before real flips. Click for Acro.

Finally, tuning. The graph is illustrative: it shows how the drone responds to a sudden stick movement. P is stiffness; it reacts to the error right now. Too much P and the drone overshoots and rings, with buzzing motors. Too little and it feels sloppy and drifts off line. I is memory; it fixes errors that linger, like wind or an off-centre battery. Too much gives a slow wobble after a move; too little and it will not hold its angle. D is damping; it brakes the motion before it overshoots. Too much amplifies sensor noise and makes motors hot; too little gives overshoot and prop-wash shaking. The method: start with I and D at zero, raise P until it rings and back off about fifteen percent, raise D until the overshoot stops while checking motor temperature, then raise I until it holds its angle. On our drone you can do all of this live from the web page.

PID tuning

Tune it live

Response to a sudden 20° stick move
4.0
1.0
0.35

Method: I and D at zero, raise P until it rings, back off 15 %. Add D until the overshoot stops. Add I until it holds its angle.

If you remember one thing from today, let it be this: measure first, then design. Prototype 1 didn't fly, and measuring the voltage at the motors is what showed us why. You can now explain how four motors steer a quad, choose a motor driver from its datasheet, read a 500 hertz control loop from IMU to PID to mixer, and spec a 6S racer and tune it safely. Good next upgrades are GPS rescue, so the drone flies home if the link drops, HD digital video, and optical flow with a barometer for hands-free hovering indoors. Questions? Then go build one. One last thing: the QR code is the repo with the firmware, these slides and my speaker notes.
